entry.title: feat(docs): rebuild the playground around someone evaluating in a tab
entry.content:
feat(docs): rebuild the playground around someone evaluating in a tab

The old page was a demo you could look at rather than one you could
evaluate. Grade the eight Korean cards and it said "nothing due, come
back tomorrow", which is the algorithm being honest and a dead end for
anyone deciding in a browser tab whether this library is worth an
afternoon. The single thing that sells spaced repetition, cards coming
back exactly when they should, was unreachable.

It was also unratable. Nobody visiting has seen 빠르다, so the only
truthful grade for every card is Again, every interval preview reads the
same, and the scheduler looks like a timer.

A time machine answers the first. Jump a day, three days, a week or a
month and the cards you graded come back on the schedule FSRS chose.
It shifts every stored timestamp backwards, which is indistinguishable
from moving "now" forwards because FSRS only ever reads elapsed time and
due-ness, and both survive a uniform shift exactly. The honest way would
be to inject a clock, since the core exports `offsetClock` for precisely
this, but `<SRSProvider>` has no clock prop yet; `demo-storage.ts` says
so, and says why it is allowed to reach past the adapter when an app
never is.

World capitals and JavaScript trivia answer the second. You genuinely
half-know eight capitals, so the grades spread and the intervals diverge.
Korean stays for anyone who wants to watch a card they keep failing.

The settings were a printed list: "FSRS, retention target 0.9, 10 cards
per sitting, interleaved". Every line of that was a real prop being
described instead of offered. Retention, session length, order and
language are now controls, and the generated snippet underneath tracks
them, so what you tuned by clicking is what you paste. Language also
gives `<RecallIntl>` its first outing anywhere in the docs.

Layout no longer jumps. Three causes, all measured:

  1. The playground was keying `<SRSProvider>` to force a fresh queue on
     every deck switch, tearing down the subtree each time. The library
     fix earlier in this branch makes the session rebuild itself, so the
     key is gone and the DOM stays put.
  2. The card (334px) and the dashboard (196px) collapsed to one-line
     loading states, taking 400px of page with them and throwing the
     scroll position away. Both hold a floor now. The loading text stays
     transparent for 350ms, so a localStorage switch says nothing and a
     slow remote adapter still explains itself.
  3. The three deck blurbs wrapped to different line counts, shifting
     everything below by 20px per click. Two lines are reserved.

Measured across 298 samples and six deck switches at both mobile and
desktop widths: zero movement. Same for the time machine. The only thing
that still resizes is the code panel gaining three lines when
`<RecallIntl>` wraps the tree, which is the code honestly being longer.

Two things the theme was hiding. The card inherited this site's absolute
`line-height: 24px` into a 30px question; one-word Korean never revealed
it, and the longer questions here would have rendered on top of each
other, so every size states its own unitless ratio now. And a card face
laid its meta pills flush against the word above them.

Retention reading 0% after a good sitting is not a bug, it counts only
mature reviews as Anki does, but it reads as broken to a newcomer. The
dashboard says so, and the one-month jump makes the figure reachable.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(react): reveal the answer with Space or Enter
entry.content:
feat(react): reveal the answer with Space or Enter

`<RatingButtons>` has always bound the number keys to the grades, on the
reasoning that serious learners grade with the keyboard and never touch
the mouse. Nothing bound reveal, so they keyed the grade and then reached
for the mouse to flip the next card, which is the keystroke they make
more often than any other. Half a keyboard interface is worse than none,
because it teaches a habit it then interrupts.

Armed only while a card is on screen and still hidden, so it can never
race the grade keys, and only in default mode, because a render prop owns
its own keyboard the same way it owns its own markup. Both keys already
mean "activate" on a focused button, link or field, and Space scrolls the
page from anywhere else, so the handler leaves those alone rather than
revealing twice or swallowing a deliberate keystroke. The button carries
`aria-keyshortcuts` so the binding is discoverable rather than folklore.

Opt out with `revealShortcut={false}`.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: fix(react): rebuild the study queue when the card set is replaced
entry.content:
fix(react): rebuild the study queue when the card set is replaced

A session held onto a queue built from cards that were no longer there.
`useStudySession` latched a `seeded` ref on the first non-empty load and
never rebuilt after it, so anything that replaced the card set afterwards
left the learner grading the old one. Switching `deckId` kept the previous
deck's queue; so did swapping the adapter, and so did an explicit
`refresh()` after a bulk import. The only escape was remounting the
provider, which is what the docs playground had resorted to.

The latch was not laziness. The hook had no way to tell apart the two
reasons `cards` changes identity, and both arrive as a brand new Map:

  1. the learner graded a card, and the queue must survive it;
  2. these are different cards now, and the queue must be thrown away.

Rebuild on both and the queue reshuffles under the learner on every
single grade. Rebuild on neither and you get this bug. So the provider
now publishes the distinction: `cardsVersion` moves once per completed
load and never on a grade, and sessions key on that.

A second half turned up while testing the first. `deckId` changes during
render, but the load answering it lands an effect and a round trip later,
and in that window the provider was serving the old deck's cards as
though they were the new deck's. A card the learner had just navigated
away from flashed up before the real one arrived. Cards now live in one
state object alongside the deck they answer and the load they came from,
so the three can never disagree, and the provider reports itself as
loading until its cards match the deck being asked for. `autoLoad={false}`
still resolves to "not loading, nothing held".

No scheduling maths is touched. A card graded Good five times in a row
gets exactly the intervals it got before; what changes is only which
cards are in the queue to be graded.

Tests are the reason for the new jsdom devDependencies: the package had
jest but no DOM, so a hook that only misbehaves across a provider
boundary could not be covered at all. They drive the real provider rather
than a stubbed context, because the failure lived in the conversation
between the two and a stub would have passed against the broken version.
Reverting the fix fails three of them and leaves "survives grading"
green, which is the shape you want.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: docs: make the public copy match what actually ships, and add an OG card
entry.content:
docs: make the public copy match what actually ships, and add an OG card

Everything a visitor reads before installing was advertising work that is
not finished, while quietly omitting work that is. Both directions cost
trust on the way in, so this squares the copy with the code.

SM-2 is scaffolded and throws, but was sold as working in the README
subtitle, core's npm description, core's README, the docs OG description,
the homepage hero pill and the repo description. It is now named only
where the comparison is fair or the copy says outright that it throws.

Two worse cases came out of the same sweep:

  - SRSProvider's `scheduler` prop documented "Defaults to SM-2". The
    default is FSRS. That JSDoc ships in the .d.ts, so editor tooltips
    were pointing every user at the scheduler that throws.
  - The algorithm page said the per-user weight optimiser "ships later".
    It is implemented in @recall-srs/core/optimizer. Replaced with the
    real API and the hold-out validation it performs.

The README's own Status table had the same problem in reverse: retention
curves, streaks, rating-button shortcuts and the optimiser were all
listed as open work despite being implemented. Only SM-2, the weight
verification and the three adapters are genuinely open.

The skeleton adapters disclosed their status in the last line of each
README, below the install and usage snippets, and not at all on npm.
Anyone copying the install line got a package where every method throws.
Status now leads: a warning block under each title pointing at
localstorage instead, "Skeleton:" at the front of each npm description,
and a badge on the adapter cards in the docs.

VERSION in the docs nav was hand-typed and stale. It rendered 0.2.0 in
the header, hero and footer while react was 0.3.0 and core 0.2.1. It now
reads from the react manifest so it cannot drift again.

Social card: there was no og:image anywhere, so every share of the repo
or the docs rendered a blank card. Built with next/og rather than
checked in as a PNG, so the headline cannot drift from the homepage.
Two things it needs to survive `output: 'export'`: `force-static`, or
the route errors, and a pinned Content-Type, because the export writes
the file with no extension and the existing nosniff header then makes
every scraper drop it.

The npm descriptions here only reach npm on the next publish.

entry.title: fix(docs): separate nav captions from nav controls, and fix the accent
entry.content:
fix(docs): separate nav captions from nav controls, and fix the accent

Three things, all in the navigation rails.

The group captions and the links beneath them were the same colour. A
caption and a control looked identical, so "Concepts" read as something
you could press. There are now three distinct levels: the caption drops
to 11px on --fg-subtle, the items sit at 13px on --fg-secondary, and the
active item keeps the raised pill and gains a marker bar.

The accent was drifting purple. --accent-soft was Korean Sunday's blue
lifted to 0.72 lightness at 0.13 chroma, which washes out into periwinkle
rather than reading as the brand colour. The brand blue itself cannot
just be dropped in as text: at 0.58 lightness it only reaches 4.1:1
against --raised, which is exactly what the active nav item sits on, so
it would fail AA on the one item most people look at. The replacement,
--accent-bright, keeps the full chroma, pulls the hue a touch off violet
and lifts only as far as legibility needs: 5.4:1 on the page, 5.2:1 on a
panel, 4.9:1 on a raised pill. Code keywords move into the same family
for the same reason.

Link underlines were inherited currentColor, so they carried whatever the
old accent was. They are now an explicit accent tint at 35% that goes to
full strength on hover, and they are always visible rather than appearing
only on hover.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Release: react 0.3.0 with localisation
entry.content:
Release: react 0.3.0 with localisation

Pins @changesets/cli back to 2.31.1. Changesets 3 requires Node 22.11+ and
this machine runs Node 20, where its version guard is buggy: it checks for
process.getBuiltinModule (Node 20 has it) then calls enableCompileCache
(Node 20 does not), so it crashes instead of reporting an unsupported
runtime.

Worth revisiting — Node 20 reached end of life in April 2026, so the real
fix is upgrading the runtime and restoring changesets 3.

react goes minor for the RecallIntl API; the other five take a patch for
README changes only. The React peer range stays ^18.2.0 || ^19.0.0 despite
the devDependency moving to 19, so React 18 users are unaffected.

Also repairs .gitignore. A `.claude/` entry had been appended as UTF-16,
so git read the whole file as binary and every rule in it silently stopped
working — which is how .claude/launch.json came to be tracked. Rewritten as
UTF-8 with LF, deduplicated, and the file untracked again.

entry.title: docs: drop the em dashes and put the logo on every README
entry.content:
docs: drop the em dashes and put the logo on every README

Two passes over the prose, kept together because they touch the same
files.

The em dashes are gone from the README, the contributing guide, the
deploy notes and all six package READMEs. Each one was repunctuated
rather than swapped for a character: a colon where a definition or list
follows, a full stop where it was really two sentences, commas or

entry.title: feat(docs): rebuild the site as a three-column documentation shell
entry.content:
feat(docs): rebuild the site as a three-column documentation shell

The site was a single centred column with a text-only nav, one prose
wrapper and an unstyled code block. It read as scaffolding rather than as
the front door of a published library.

Structure:

- A three-column docs shell: page tree, content, section list. The rail
  is two elements on purpose. The outer column carries the surface and
  the divider and is a plain flex child, so it stretches the height of
  the section and stops where the footer begins. A sticky element cannot
  do that, because at the end of a page it stays pinned at viewport
  height and its background hangs in mid-air above the footer.
- "On this page" builds itself from the rendered article and assigns the
  heading ids, so pages stay plain JSX with no frontmatter to maintain.
  It is keyed on the pathname because the layout survives client-side
  navigation; without that the rail keeps the first page's headings and
  no later page ever gets ids.
- Cmd-K search. The index is built on first open by fetching each page
  and reading its headings out of the HTML, so it cannot drift from the
  content and needs no build step.
- Numbered steps, a prev/next pager and a section rail, all driven by
  `lib/nav.ts` so a new page is one entry rather than four edits.

Visual language, following Linear's redesign notes: hierarchy comes from
four surface elevations and four text levels rather than from large type
or decoration, one typeface throughout with headings differing by weight
and tracking, and 13px interface chrome against 15px prose.

The accents are the two taegeuk colours carried over from Korean Sunday,
used under the same rule that app follows: blue marks where you are and
how far you have got, red is spent only on the action to take next. That
is why the primary button and "Show answer" are red while navigation,
links and the active section marker are blue.

`lib/highlight.ts` is a small tokeniser rather than a syntax highlighting
dependency. The site's only dependencies are still next and react.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat: add the Recall logo and favicon assets
entry.content:
feat: add the Recall logo and favicon assets

The site had no favicon, no touch icon and no mark anywhere, so a tab
showed the default globe and the READMEs opened on a bare heading.

Two forms of the mark are committed because they are used on backgrounds
that are nothing alike:

- Transparent PNGs under `packages/docs/public/brand/`, for the site,
  which sits on a near-black canvas.
- A dark rounded tile under `docs/media/`, for GitHub and npm, which
  render READMEs on white. A transparent version there would show dark
  fringing and the off-white wordmark would nearly vanish.

`favicon.ico`, `icon.png` and `apple-icon.png` go in `app/` so Next's
file conventions emit the link tags, rather than hand-written head markup
that can drift. The touch icon is opaque on #08090A because iOS
composites it onto its own background.

The source artwork was a screen capture, so the sizes stop at 128px. That
is comfortably enough for a 48px favicon and a 20px header mark, both of
which are heavy downscales, but it is not enough for a 512px store icon
or a 1200x630 social card. Those are deliberately absent rather than
shipped soft, and want a vector or 1024px export first.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: build: upgrade to Next 16, React 19, Tailwind 4 and ESLint 10
entry.content:
build: upgrade to Next 16, React 19, Tailwind 4 and ESLint 10

The docs site was on Next 14 and Tailwind 3, and the repo still used an
`.eslintrc.json` that ESLint 10 no longer reads. This moves the whole
workspace onto current majors and rewrites the theme for Tailwind's
CSS-first config, which is the same shape the other projects in this
account already use.

Two places do not go to the latest version, both because the toolchain
around them caps it:

- TypeScript stays on 5.9.3. typescript-eslint requires `<6.1.0` and
  ts-jest requires `<7`, so TypeScript 7 breaks linting and the test run.
- size-limit stays on 12.x. Version 13 and up need `fs/promises.glob`,
  which lands in Node 22, and the packages still claim `>=18.17`.

ESLint 10 itself needs Node >=20.19, so CI now skips the lint step on the
Node 18 matrix row. Typecheck and tests still run there, which is what
actually backs the core's Node 18 support claim.

Tailwind 4 moves the theme into CSS, so `tailwind.config.ts` is gone and
the tokens live in `globals.css` under `@theme inline`. The component
theme moves out to `recall-theme.css` and is now plain CSS with no
Tailwind at all, so it can be copied into any project, which is the whole
point of shipping a worked example.

entry.title: Add internationalisation to the default components
entry.content:
Add internationalisation to the default components

The engine was always language-agnostic — `question` and `answer` are
opaque strings the scheduler never reads — but the components shipped
hardcoded English, which is an odd thing to hand to people building
language-learning apps. Translating the UI meant abandoning the default
components for a render prop.

Two layers:

- Label props on StudyView (revealLabel, skipLabel, restartLabel) for
  one-off wording on a single screen.
- <RecallIntl locale strings> for the whole tree. `strings` is a deep
  partial, so overriding three keys leaves the rest English rather than
  blank. No provider needed: components fall back to English and the
  runtime locale, so nothing breaks for existing users.

Numbers go through Intl.NumberFormat with style:'unit' rather than string
concatenation, so `locale` alone produces "3 j", "3 T", "3 dias" and the
right decimal separator without this package shipping a translation table
for every unit in every language. Intl.RelativeTimeFormat is the tempting
alternative and wrong — it yields "in 3 days", and a rating button needs a
quantity, not a sentence. An invalid locale degrades to English instead of
throwing mid-render.

14 tests, run against real locales rather than a mocked Intl: the whole
point is that the platform knows French and we do not.

README also gains a "Where this came from" section — the engine comes from
Korean Sunday, built for the gaps between Korean classes.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Set framework null explicitly so Vercel serves the static export
entry.content:
Set framework null explicitly so Vercel serves the static export

Omitting the key leaves the project's saved framework (Next.js) in place,
and the Next builder then looks for `next` in the root package.json,
which a monorepo does not have. Explicit null overrides it.
